name: Radithor

lead: Radithor was a bottled tonic of distilled water containing radium-226 and radium-228, made by Bailey Radium Laboratories of East Orange, New Jersey and sold in the 1920s. It was marketed as a way to stimulate the body, restore vitality and treat a long list of ailments, in an era when weak radioactivity was widely believed to invigorate and rejuvenate.

It appears in beauty and longevity history because the period's radioactive tonics, waters and cosmetics were promoted for rejuvenation and improved appearance. The best-known user, industrialist Eben Byers, died in 1932 after drinking large quantities, a case that pushed public and regulatory attitudes against radioactive patent medicines.

paras: Historically it was sold by mail order and through pharmacies in small bottles taken by mouth, with promotional materials encouraging regular daily use. The product is no longer made.

Radium lodges in bone and emits alpha radiation. Byers developed cancers and lost his jaw before dying in 1932, and a later analysis estimated his cumulative skeletal dose may have exceeded 350 Sv. Radioactive patent medicines declined after his death.

angle.text: Radithor was sold as a daily tonic to restore energy and vitality, part of a 1920s wave of radioactive products promoted for rejuvenation and beauty. It is documented today as a historical case rather than a current practice.

lead: Radithor was a radioactive patent medicine consisting of distilled water containing at least 1 microcurie each of radium-226 and radium-228, sold in half-ounce bottles by Bailey Radium Laboratories of East Orange, New Jersey, owned by William J. A. Bailey.[1] It sold about 400,000 bottles between 1925 and 1930.[1]

It belonged to the era of 'mild radium therapy', in which practitioners and manufacturers promoted small doses of radium and its decay products for rheumatic conditions, hypertension and metabolic disorders.[2] A German historical study describes radioactive drugs, foodstuffs and cosmetics of the first half of the twentieth century as marketed with the belief that weak radiation stimulated vital forces, supporting recovery, beauty and rejuvenation.[3]

Radithor was advertised under slogans such as 'Perpetual Sunshine' and as a remedy for impotence and many other ailments.[1] The 1932 death of golfer and industrialist Eben Byers, who reportedly drank around 1,400 bottles from 1927, became its defining episode.[1] The FDA warned against it but, at the time, lacked authority to ban it.[1]

paras: Radithor was introduced as a tonic by Bailey Radium Laboratories, which Wikipedia reports ran from 1918; the company was run by William J. A. Bailey, who was not a medical doctor.[1] Its marketing described a 'cure for the living dead' and promised that mild radioactivity would stimulate metabolism.[1] It was expensive relative to other tonics and sold well among affluent buyers.[1][2]

Eben Byers, a Yale-educated Pittsburgh industrialist and amateur golf champion, began taking Radithor in 1927 and reportedly consumed about 1,400 bottles.[1] He died in 1932 of cancers after surgery to remove his jaw; when his body was exhumed in 1965 it was still radioactive.[1]

A 1990 JAMA analysis of original Radithor samples and a computer model estimated Byers's cumulative skeletal radiation dose at more than 350 Sv, far above levels considered rapidly lethal if given at once, with alpha emitters concentrated in bone.[4] The case helped strengthen US regulation of drugs and radioactive products, and the 1938 Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act expanded FDA authority.[1]

Promoters claimed Radithor energised the body and treated impotence, rheumatism, hypertension and many other conditions.[1][2] Contemporary radioactive products also included bath waters and cosmetics promoted for beauty and rejuvenation.[3]
No studies found. Historical analyses of the product's radiotoxicology and of the mild radium therapy era exist.[2][4]
Radithor is cited in medical histories as a case study of how narratives sustain pseudocures and panaceas.[5]

timeline.event: Bailey Radium Laboratories begins manufacturing (as reported by Wikipedia).[1]
